representative_questions.question: How does the degree of coverage of the PPE phase by Janus particles affect the CO2 mass uptake of the blend?
representative_questions.expected_answer: Partial coverage (1 and 2 wt% JPs) increases CO2 uptake due to stress concentration and the formation of microcrazes/cracks that increase available surface area, whereas full coverage (5 and 10 wt% JPs) reduces uptake as the JPs act as a barrier layer hindering diffusion into the PPE phase.

representative_questions.question: How does the amount of Janus particles (JPs) affect the morphology of the PPE/SAN blend and the resulting CO2 mass uptake?
representative_questions.expected_answer: Low amounts of JPs (1-2 wt%) result in partial coverage of PPE domains, creating stress concentration points and microcrazes that increase CO2 mass uptake. Higher amounts (5-10 wt%) lead to full coverage of PPE droplets (raspberry morphology), which acts as a barrier layer and decreases CO2 mass uptake.

representative_questions.question: How does the concentration of Janus particles (JPs) influence the average cell size of PPE/SAN blend foams, and what is the specific JP content that yields the lowest cell size?
representative_questions.expected_answer: The average foam cell size decreases with increasing amount of JP because smaller PPE domain sizes provide increased foam nucleation sites. The lowest cell size (900 nm) is achieved with the blend compatibilized with 5 wt% JPs.

representative_questions.question: How does the CO2-induced reduction in glass transition temperature (Tg) of neat PPE compare to the reported reduction of polystyrene (PS) at 40 bar?
representative_questions.expected_answer: The Tg of neat PPE is reduced by 24 °C at 40 bar, while the Tg of PS is reported to decrease by around 30 °C at the same pressure.

merged_from.question: How does the degree of coverage of the PPE phase by Janus nanoparticles affect the carbon dioxide sorption behavior and the resulting foam morphology?
merged_from.expected_answer: Partial coverage of the PPE phase results in stress concentration at the blend interface during saturation, leading to the formation of new surfaces via cleavage or microcrazes, which increases CO2 sorption. In contrast, full coverage (raspberry morphology) creates a barrier layer due to the lower CO2 solubility of the cross-linked PB core, hindering gas entrance into the PPE phase and resulting in homogenous foams with small cell sizes and relatively high densities.

representative_questions.question: How does the concentration of Janus particles (JPs) affect the CO2 mass uptake in PPE/SAN blends?
representative_questions.expected_answer: CO2 uptake first increases at low concentrations (1 and 2 wt% JPs) due to stress concentration and the formation of microcrazes/cracks that increase available surface area, but then decreases at higher concentrations (5 and 10 wt% JPs) because the PPE phase is fully covered, eliminating stress points and creating a barrier layer via the PB core.
representative_questions.why_kept: Only question of this type; no merge

representative_questions.question: How does the foam morphology produced using Janus particles compare to that of the neat PPE/SAN blend?
representative_questions.expected_answer: The neat blend nearly did not foam and could not be properly evaluated, whereas the use of Janus particles produced homogenous foams characterized by small cell sizes (down to below 1 mm with 5 wt% JP) and relatively high densities (350–650 kg m-3).
representative_questions.why_kept: Only question of this type; no merge

representative_questions.question: Why was the temperature for the CO2 mass uptake experiments specifically set to 40 °C?
representative_questions.expected_answer: This temperature was chosen due to the lower critical solution temperature (LCST) behavior of PMMA, which is partially present in the Janus particles and at the blend interface.
representative_questions.why_kept: Only question of this type; no merge

representative_questions.question: What is the relationship between the coverage of the PPE phase by Janus particles and the resulting foam cell size?
representative_questions.expected_answer: Higher JP content (5 and 10 wt%) leads to full coverage of the PPE phase, which reduces the PPE domain size and increases the surface available for nucleation, resulting in a visible decrease in mean cell size compared to blends with lower JP amounts.
representative_questions.why_kept: Only question of this type; no merge

representative_questions.expected_answer: Due to technical difficulties, it was not possible to measure SAN at 35 bar (because of its lower Tg) and the other materials at 40 bar, which was the actual CO2 mass uptake pressure.

representative_questions.question: How does the effect of Janus particles on the morphology of PPE/SAN blends compare to that of neat (uncompatibilized) blends as reported in the results?
representative_questions.expected_answer: Janus particles result in finer morphologies with significantly reduced PPE droplet diameters (down to ~300 nm) and more homogeneous distributions compared to the irregular-shaped domains seen in neat blends.
